```{r}
library(simpexp)
```

## The idea

A hazard that is constant on the intervals of a grid determines everything else
in closed form. Its cumulative hazard is piecewise linear, so the waiting time
can be drawn by inverting it exactly; and when several transitions compete,
the hazards are constant within the interval in which the event falls, so the
transition that is realised can be drawn with probabilities proportional to
them. No quadrature, no root finding, no rejection step.

The grid is therefore part of the model, not a numerical tuning parameter.
A hazard that varies quickly needs a fine grid to be represented faithfully --
and the same grid is the one on which piecewise exponential additive models are
fitted, which is what makes simulation and estimation speak about the same
quantities.

## Three interfaces, one engine

Everything is specified by a one-sided formula for the **log**-hazard.

### A single event

```{r}
df  <- data.frame(x = rnorm(500), trt = rbinom(500, 1, 0.5))
cut <- seq(0, 10, by = 0.1)

sim <- sim_pexp(~ log(0.1) + 0.05 * t + 0.7 * trt - 0.3 * x, df, cut = cut)
head(sim)
```

The output is always in the same long format: one row per episode, with
`tstart`, `tstop`, `from`, `to`, `status` and the covariates of the input data.
`status = 0` marks an episode that ended without a transition, and then `to` is
`NA`. For a single event that is all there is to it -- one episode per subject.

```{r}
mean(sim$status)
```

A hazard given as one value per interval needs no closed form at all; the
variable `interval` is the index of the current interval of `cut`:

```{r}
rates <- c(0.05, 0.2, 0.35, 0.2, 0.1)
sim_pexp(~ log(rates[interval]) + 0.5 * trt, df, cut = c(0, 1, 2, 4, 7, 10)) |>
  head(3)
```

### Competing risks

One formula per cause; the names become the cause labels.

```{r}
cr <- sim_pexp_cr(
  list(relapse = ~ log(0.1) + 0.5 * trt,
       death   = ~ log(0.03) - 0.2 * x),
  df, cut = cut)
table(cr$to, useNA = "ifany")
```

`to` is `NA` exactly for the administratively censored subjects, which is
`status == 0`.

### Multi-state processes

A transition is the triple (origin, target, log-hazard). States may recur: the
engine keeps drawing until every subject has reached a terminal state, been
censored, or run out of follow-up.

```{r}
msm_sim <- sim_pexp_msm(
  list(
    transition("healthy", "ill",     ~ log(0.4) + 0.3 * x),
    transition("healthy", "dead",    ~ log(0.02)),
    transition("ill",     "healthy", ~ log(0.8)),
    transition("ill",     "dead",    ~ log(0.05) + 0.15 * t_sojourn)
  ),
  df, cut = cut)

head(msm_sim, 8)
table(msm_sim$transition, useNA = "ifany")
```

States that have no outgoing transition are terminal by default (`dead` here);
`terminal_states` overrides that.

```{r}
# how often subjects pass through `ill`
table(table(msm_sim$id[msm_sim$to == "ill" & !is.na(msm_sim$to)]))
```

## Starting elsewhere, starting later

Two optional columns of `data` control where a subject starts: `from` gives the
initial state and `t_entry` the time at which it was entered. The first
interval of such a subject starts at its entry time, so entering in the middle
of an interval is handled exactly rather than rounded to the grid.

```{r}
staggered <- data.frame(
  id      = 1:6,
  x       = 0,
  from    = c("healthy", "healthy", "ill", "ill", "ill", "healthy"),
  t_entry = c(0, 0, 1.37, 2.5, 4, 0))

sim_pexp_msm(
  list(
    transition("healthy", "ill",  ~ log(0.4)),
    transition("ill",     "dead", ~ log(0.2))),
  staggered, cut = seq(0, 10, by = 0.5)) |>
  subset(select = c(id, episode, from, to, tstart, tstop, status))
```

## Fitting what was simulated

The point of simulating on a grid is that the same grid carries over to
estimation. Expand the episodes into intervals, fit a Poisson model with the
log of the interval length as offset, and the coefficients are the ones that
were put in.

```{r}
truth <- c(intercept = log(0.2), trt = 0.7, x = -0.3)
dat   <- data.frame(x = rnorm(3000), trt = rbinom(3000, 1, 0.5))
sim   <- sim_pexp(~ log(0.2) + 0.7 * trt - 0.3 * x, dat, cut = seq(0, 10, by = 0.5))

# one row per subject and interval at risk
expand <- function(sim, cut) {
  lo <- cut[-length(cut)]; hi <- cut[-1L]
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(lo), function(j) {
    at_risk <- sim$tstop > lo[j]
    d <- sim[at_risk, , drop = FALSE]
    d$offset <- log(pmin(d$tstop, hi[j]) - lo[j])
    d$event  <- as.integer(d$status == 1L & d$tstop <= hi[j])
    d$j      <- j
    d
  }))
}
ped <- expand(sim, seq(0, 10, by = 0.5))

fit <- glm(event ~ trt + x, offset = offset, family = poisson(), data = ped)
cbind(truth = truth, estimate = coef(fit), confint.default(fit))
```

A constant baseline hazard was simulated, so no baseline term is needed here.
With a time-varying baseline, `j` (or a smooth function of interval midpoints)
goes into the model -- that is precisely a piecewise exponential additive
model.
